<flow name="EmailSystemArchitecture" category="DOC/GUIDE" spid="foam" description="Architecture overview of FOAM3's email pipeline: config entry types, rule-driven processing, templates, Microsoft Graph integration." keywords="email,architecture,templates,microsoft graph,knowledge"/>

# FOAM3 Email System Architecture

## Table of Contents
1. [Quick Start](#quick-start)
2. [Overview](#overview)
3. [Architecture](#architecture)
4. [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
5. [Configuration Classes](#configuration-classes)
6. [Email Agents](#email-agents)
7. [Property Service Chain](#property-service-chain)
8. [Template System](#template-system)
9. [Rule Engine Integration](#rule-engine-integration)
10. [DAOs and Data Flow](#daos-and-data-flow)
11. [Microsoft Graph Integration](#microsoft-graph-integration)
12. [Gotchas](#gotchas)

---

## Quick Start

1. Create an `EmailServiceConfig` entry in `emailServiceConfig.jrl` with SMTP credentials
2. Create `EmailTemplate` entries in `emailTemplates.jrl` with your email body/subject
3. Create `EmailConfig` entry in `emailConfig.jrl` for per-SPID defaults
4. Put an `EmailMessage` with `status: DRAFT` to `emailMessageDAO` - the system handles the rest

### What Are These Configuration Entries?

```
+-------------------+     +-------------------+     +-------------------+
| EmailServiceConfig|     | EmailTemplate     |     | EmailConfig       |
+-------------------+     +-------------------+     +-------------------+
| HOW to send       |     | WHAT to send      |     | WHO sends it      |
|                   |     |                   |     |                   |
| - SMTP host/port  |     | - Subject         |     | - from address    |
| - Credentials     |     | - Body HTML       |     | - replyTo address |
| - TLS settings    |     | - Variables       |     | - displayName     |
| - Poll interval   |     | - Per group/locale|     | - Per SPID        |
+-------------------+     +-------------------+     +-------------------+
```

**EmailServiceConfig** - "How to connect to the mail server"

The connection configuration that tells the system HOW to send emails: SMTP host, port, username/password, TLS settings. Think of it as the mail server login credentials.

**EmailTemplate** - "What the email looks like"

The email content - the actual subject and body with variable placeholders like `{{ userName }}`. Templates can vary by group, locale, and SPID. Think of it as a reusable email blueprint.

**EmailConfig** - "Who sends the email"

The sender defaults per SPID (tenant) - default `from`, `replyTo`, and `displayName` values. Think of it as the "From:" line defaults for each tenant.

---

## Overview

### What It Does

The FOAM3 Email System is a comprehensive, rule-driven email processing pipeline that:

- **Sends emails** via SMTP or Microsoft Graph API
- **Receives emails** via IMAP/POP3 protocols
- **Processes templates** with variable substitution and inheritance
- **Applies cascading configuration** from theme, group, and SPID sources
- **Validates messages** before sending
- **Throttles delivery** to respect provider rate limits
- **Tracks status** through the complete email lifecycle

### Key Files

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `EmailMessage.js` | Core email data model with status tracking |
| `EmailServiceConfig.js` | SMTP/IMAP connection configuration |
| `EmailTemplate.js` | Reusable email templates with variable support |
| `EmailConfig.js` | Per-SPID default sender configuration |
| `SMTPAgent.js` | SMTP sending agent (polls for UNSENT emails) |
| `EmailFolderAgent.js` | IMAP receiving agent (polls for new emails) |
| `MicrosoftGraphEmailAgent.js` | Microsoft 365 sending via Graph API |
| `ChainedPropertyService.js` | Orchestrates the property service pipeline |
| `EmailTemplateEngine.js` | Template variable substitution engine |
| `EmailTemplateSupport.java` | Template lookup with fallback logic |

---

## Architecture

### High-Level System Architecture

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                              FOAM3 Email System                                    |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                                   |
|  +-------------------------+     +-------------------------+                      |
|  |   EMAIL CREATION        |     |   EMAIL RECEIVING       |                      |
|  |  (Notification/Direct)  |     |   (IMAP/POP3)          |                      |
|  +------------+------------+     +------------+------------+                      |
|               |                               |                                   |
|               v                               v                                   |
|  +------------+------------+     +------------+------------+                      |
|  |  emailMessageDAO        |     | emailMessageReceivedDAO |                      |
|  |  (status: DRAFT)        |     | (status: RECEIVED)      |                      |
|  +------------+------------+     +------------+------------+                      |
|               |                               |                                   |
|               v                               v                                   |
|  +------------+---------------------------------------------------+              |
|  |                      RULE ENGINE                                |              |
|  |  +------------------+  +------------------+  +----------------+ |              |
|  |  | PropertyService  |  | Status Rule      |  | Processed Rule | |              |
|  |  | Rule (pri:1000)  |  | (pri:100)        |  | (pri:0)        | |              |
|  |  +------------------+  +------------------+  +----------------+ |              |
|  +----------------------------------------------------------------+              |
|               |                                                                   |
|               v                                                                   |
|  +------------+------------+                                                      |
|  |  emailMessageDAO        |                                                      |
|  |  (status: UNSENT)       |                                                      |
|  +------------+------------+                                                      |
|               |                                                                   |
|               v                                                                   |
|  +------------+-------------------------------------------+                       |
|  |                   EMAIL AGENTS                          |                       |
|  |  +----------------+  +----------------+  +------------+ |                       |
|  |  |  SMTPAgent     |  | MSGraphAgent   |  | FolderAgent| |                       |
|  |  |  (id: smtp)    |  | (id: msGraph)  |  | (id: imap) | |                       |
|  |  +----------------+  +----------------+  +------------+ |                       |
|  +--------------------------------------------------------+                       |
|               |                                                                   |
|               v                                                                   |
|  +------------+------------+                                                      |
|  |   EXTERNAL SERVERS      |                                                      |
|  |  SMTP / Graph API       |                                                      |
|  +-------------------------+                                                      |
|                                                                                   |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Property Service Chain Architecture

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        ChainedPropertyService                                      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                                   |
|   EmailMessage (DRAFT)                                                            |
|        |                                                                          |
|        v                                                                          |
|   +----+------------------------------------------+                               |
|   | 1. ApplyBaseArgumentsEmailPropertyService     |                               |
|   |    - Sets SPID from user                      |                               |
|   |    - Loads theme, appConfig, supportConfig    |                               |
|   |    - Populates templateArgs (logo, appLink,   |                               |
|   |      supportEmail, hostname, etc.)            |                               |
|   +-----------------------------------------------+                               |
|        |                                                                          |
|        v                                                                          |
|   +----+------------------------------------------+                               |
|   | 2. EmailTemplateApplyEmailPropertyService     |                               |
|   |    - Finds EmailTemplate by name/group/locale |                               |
|   |    - Applies template to emailMessage         |                               |
|   |    - Renders body, subject with variables     |                               |
|   +-----------------------------------------------+                               |
|        |                                                                          |
|        v                                                                          |
|   +----+------------------------------------------+                               |
|   | 3. GroupEmailTemplateService                  |                               |
|   |    - Walks group hierarchy for replyTo, from  |                               |
|   |    - Inherits from parent groups              |                               |
|   +-----------------------------------------------+                               |
|        |                                                                          |
|        v                                                                          |
|   +----+------------------------------------------+                               |
|   | 4. EmailConfigEmailPropertyService            |                               |
|   |    - Loads EmailConfig by SPID                |                               |
|   |    - Sets replyTo, displayName, from, to      |                               |
|   +-----------------------------------------------+                               |
|        |                                                                          |
|        v                                                                          |
|   +----+------------------------------------------+                               |
|   | 5. EmailMessageValidationPropertyService      |                               |
|   |    - Validates: to, subject, body are set     |                               |
|   |    - Throws InvalidParameterException if not  |                               |
|   +-----------------------------------------------+                               |
|        |                                                                          |
|        v                                                                          |
|   EmailMessage (validated, ready for UNSENT)                                      |
|                                                                                   |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

---

## Key Concepts

### Email Status Lifecycle

| Status | Ordinal | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| DRAFT | 0 | Initial state - triggers rule processing |
| UNSENT | 1 | Processed and validated - ready for agent pickup |
| SENT | 2 | Successfully delivered to mail server |
| FAILED | 3 | Delivery failed (permanent) |
| BOUNCED | 4 | Message bounced back |
| RECEIVED | 5 | Inbound email received via IMAP/POP3 |
| PROCESSED | 6 | Received email has been processed |

### Configuration Hierarchy

Configuration values are resolved in order of precedence (first match wins):

1. **EmailMessage** - explicitly set properties on the message
2. **EmailTemplate** - template-level defaults
3. **Group** - user's group hierarchy (walks up to root)
4. **EmailConfig** - SPID-level defaults
5. **Theme/SupportConfig** - theme-level defaults

### Template Variable Substitution

The EmailTemplateEngine supports three syntax patterns:

| Syntax | Purpose | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `{{ variable }}` | Simple variable substitution | `{{ appName }}` |
| `{{ object.property }}` | Object property access | `{{ user.firstName }}` |
| `{% if var %}...{% endif %}` | Conditional blocks | `{% if showLogo %}...{% endif %}` |
| `{% if var %}...{% else %}...{% endif %}` | Conditional with else | `{% if premium %}...{% else %}...{% endif %}` |
| `{$ tokenName $}` | CSS token substitution | `{$ primary500 $}` |
| `<include template='name'>...</include>` | Template inheritance | See Template Inheritance section |

---

## Configuration Classes

### EmailServiceConfig

Base configuration for email service connections (SMTP/IMAP).

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| id | String | 'default' | Unique identifier (e.g., 'smtp', 'imap', 'msGraph') |
| enabled | Boolean | false | Whether this config is active |
| host | String | '127.0.0.1' | Mail server hostname |
| port | String | '587' | Mail server port |
| username | String | null | Authentication username |
| password | Password | null | Authentication password |
| authenticate | Boolean | true | Whether to use authentication |
| starttls | Boolean | true | Whether to use STARTTLS |
| protocol | String | 'smtp' | Protocol: 'smtp' or 'imaps' |
| pollInterval | Long | 10000 | Agent polling interval (ms) |
| initialDelay | Int | 60000 | Agent startup delay (ms) |
| folderName | String | 'INBOX' | Folder to fetch (IMAP only) |
| delete | Boolean | false | Delete after fetch (IMAP only) |
| processAttachments | Boolean | true | Process attachments (IMAP only) |

### EmailServiceConfig (Microsoft Graph Extension)

Additional properties for Microsoft Graph API authentication.

| Property | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| clientId | String | Microsoft Graph API client ID |
| tenantId | String | Microsoft Graph API tenant ID |
| password | String | Client secret (uses base class password field) |

### EmailConfig

Per-SPID email defaults (keyed by SPID).

| Property | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| spid | Reference | Service Provider ID (primary key) |
| from | String | Default sender email address |
| displayName | String | Default sender display name |
| replyTo | String | Default reply-to address |

### EmailTemplate

Reusable email templates with variable support.

| Property | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| id | String | Unique identifier |
| name | String | Template name (used for lookup) |
| group | String | Group filter ('*' for all) |
| locale | String | Locale filter ('en' default) |
| spid | String | SPID filter (empty for all) |
| subject | String | Email subject (supports variables) |
| body | String | Email body HTML (supports variables) |
| displayName | String | Sender display name |
| sendTo | String | Default recipient |
| replyTo | String | Reply-to address |
| enabled | Boolean | Whether template is active |
| sourceClass | String | Tracking: which class uses this template |

### EmailMessage

The core email data model.

| Property | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| id | String | Unique message identifier |
| user | Reference | Target user for this email |
| status | Enum | Current status (DRAFT, UNSENT, SENT, etc.) |
| from | String | Sender address |
| displayName | String | Sender display name |
| replyTo | String | Reply-to address |
| to | StringArray | Recipient addresses |
| cc | StringArray | CC addresses |
| bcc | StringArray | BCC addresses |
| subject | String | Email subject |
| body | String | Email body (HTML) |
| templateArguments | Map | Variables for template rendering |
| attachments | StringArray | File IDs for attachments |
| sentDate | DateTime | When the email was sent |
| created | DateTime | When the message was created |
| spid | Reference | Service provider ID |

---

## Email Agents

### SMTPAgent

The primary sending agent for SMTP protocol.

**Service ID:** `smtp` (references EmailServiceConfig with id='smtp')

**Behavior:**
1. Starts a timer on `start()` using config's `initialDelay` and `pollInterval`
2. On each execution cycle:
   - Queries `emailMessageDAO` for messages with `status=UNSENT`
   - For each message, throttles (via `smtpAgentThrottle`), then sends
   - Updates message status to SENT or FAILED
3. Maintains SMTP session/transport for connection reuse
4. Auto-disables on repeated authentication failures
5. Reloads configuration if it changes between polling cycles

**Key Methods:**
- `start()` - Initialize timer and begin polling
- `stop()` - Cancel timer
- `execute()` - Process unsent emails
- `send()` - Send individual email via SMTP
- `createMimeMessage()` - Convert EmailMessage to MimeMessage
- `reload()` - Hot-reload configuration changes

### EmailFolderAgent

The receiving agent for IMAP/POP3 protocols.

**Service ID:** `imap` (references EmailServiceConfig with id='imap')

**Behavior:**
1. Starts a timer on `start()` using config's `initialDelay` and `pollInterval`
2. On each execution cycle:
   - Connects to mail server using config credentials
   - Opens configured folder (default: INBOX)
   - Searches for unread messages
   - For each message:
     - Converts to EmailMessage (status=RECEIVED)
     - Processes attachments (saves to fileDAO)
     - Looks up sender user by email
     - Puts to `emailMessageReceivedDAO`
     - Marks as SEEN or deletes based on config
3. Closes connection after each cycle

### MicrosoftGraphEmailAgent

Sending agent for Microsoft 365 via Graph API (extends SMTPAgent).

**Service ID:** `msGraph` (references ms.EmailServiceConfig with id='msGraph')

**Behavior:**
1. Uses OAuth2 client credentials flow for authentication
2. Acquires access token with scope `https://outlook.office365.com/.default`
3. Sends via Exchange Web Services (EWS) with OAuth bearer token
4. Automatically refreshes token when within 5 minutes of expiry
5. Uses impersonation header for app-only token scenarios
6. Throttles via `microsoftGraphEmailAgentThrottle` (default: 4 TPS)

**Configuration Requirements:**
- `clientId` - Azure AD application client ID
- `tenantId` - Azure AD tenant ID
- `password` - Client secret
- `username` - Email address to send from (for impersonation)

---

## Property Service Chain

The `emailPropertyService` is a `ChainedPropertyService` that processes each EmailMessage through a pipeline of services. Each service in the chain can modify the email, adding properties that weren't already set.

### Service Order and Responsibilities

| Order | Service | Priority | Responsibility |
|-------|---------|----------|----------------|
| 1 | ApplyBaseArgumentsEmailPropertyService | Highest | Sets SPID, loads theme/support config, populates base templateArgs |
| 2 | EmailTemplateApplyEmailPropertyService | - | Finds template, renders body/subject/displayName/replyTo/sendTo |
| 3 | GroupEmailTemplateService | - | Inherits replyTo/displayName/from from group hierarchy |
| 4 | EmailConfigEmailPropertyService | - | Applies per-SPID defaults from EmailConfig |
| 5 | EmailMessageValidationPropertyService | Lowest | Validates required fields (to, subject, body) |

### Built-in Template Arguments

The `ApplyBaseArgumentsEmailPropertyService` automatically populates these variables:

| Variable | Source | Description |
|----------|--------|-------------|
| logo | Theme | URL to theme logo |
| largeLogo | Theme | URL to large theme logo |
| appLink | AppConfig | Application base URL |
| appName | Theme | Application name |
| locale | User | User's language code |
| supportAddress | SupportConfig | Support postal address |
| supportPhone | SupportConfig | Support phone number |
| supportEmail | SupportConfig | Support email address |
| supportLogo | SupportConfig | Support logo URL |
| termsAndCondLink | AppConfig | Terms and conditions URL |
| termsAndCondLabel | AppConfig | Terms and conditions label |
| copyright | AppConfig | Copyright text |
| privacyUrl | AppConfig | Privacy policy URL |
| privacyLabel | AppConfig | Privacy policy label |
| personalSupportPhone | SupportConfig | Personal support user phone |
| personalSupportEmail | SupportConfig | Personal support user email |
| personalSupportFirstName | SupportConfig | Personal support user first name |
| personalSupportFullName | SupportConfig | Personal support user full name |
| hostname | System | Server hostname |
| theme | Theme | Full theme object for advanced use |

---

## Template System

### Template Lookup Logic

The `EmailTemplateSupport.findTemplate()` method searches for templates with cascading fallback:

```
Search Order (first match wins):
+-------+-------+--------+------+
| Name  | Group | Locale | SPID |
+-------+-------+--------+------+
|   Y   |   Y   |   Y    |   Y  |  <- Most specific
|   Y   |   Y   |   Y    |   *  |
|   Y   |   Y   |   en   |   Y  |
|   Y   |   Y   |   en   |   *  |
|   Y   | parent|   Y    |   Y  |  <- Walk group hierarchy
|   Y   | parent|   Y    |   *  |
|   Y   | parent|   en   |   Y  |
|   Y   | parent|   en   |   *  |
|   Y   |   *   |   en   |   Y  |
|   Y   |   *   |   en   |   *  |  <- Least specific (catch-all)
+-------+-------+--------+------+
```

### Template Inheritance

Templates can extend other templates using the `<include>` tag:

```
Parent Template (base-email):
+----------------------------------+
| <html>                           |
|   <head>...</head>               |
|   <body>                         |
|     <header>Logo</header>        |
|     <content></content>          |  <- Insertion point
|     <footer>Copyright</footer>   |
|   </body>                        |
| </html>                          |
+----------------------------------+

Child Template (welcome-email):
+----------------------------------+
| <include template='base-email'>  |
|   <h1>Welcome!</h1>              |
|   <p>Hello {{ userName }}</p>    |
| </include>                       |
+----------------------------------+

Rendered Result:
+----------------------------------+
| <html>                           |
|   <head>...</head>               |
|   <body>                         |
|     <header>Logo</header>        |
|     <h1>Welcome!</h1>            |
|     <p>Hello John</p>            |
|     <footer>Copyright</footer>   |
|   </body>                        |
| </html>                          |
+----------------------------------+
```

---

## Rule Engine Integration

### Email Rules

Three rules process emails on `localEmailMessageDAO`:

| Rule ID | Priority | Predicate | Action | Purpose |
|---------|----------|-----------|--------|---------|
| EmailMessagePropertyServiceRule | 1000 | status=DRAFT | EmailMessagePropertyServiceRuleAction | Process through property service chain |
| EmailMessageStatusRule | 100 | status=DRAFT | EmailMessageStatusRuleAction | Set status to UNSENT |
| EmailMessageProcessedStatusRule | 0 | status=PROCESSED | DAOPutRuleAction | Move to emailMessageProcessedDAO |

### Rule Execution Flow

```
EmailMessage PUT (status: DRAFT)
        |
        v
+-------+-------+
| Rule Engine   |
| daoKey:       |
| localEmail-   |
| MessageDAO    |
+-------+-------+
        |
        | Priority 1000
        v
+-------+-------+
| PropertySvc   |
| Rule          |
| - Apply chain |
| - Render      |
|   template    |
| - Validate    |
+-------+-------+
        |
        | Priority 100
        v
+-------+-------+
| Status Rule   |
| - Set status  |
|   to UNSENT   |
+-------+-------+
        |
        v
EmailMessage (status: UNSENT)
        |
        v
SMTPAgent picks up and sends
```

---

## DAOs and Data Flow

### Email DAOs

| DAO | Purpose | Journal |
|-----|---------|---------|
| localEmailTemplateDAO | Template storage | emailTemplates |
| emailTemplateDAO | Template access (wraps local) | - |
| localEmailMessageDAO | Outbound message storage | emailMessages |
| emailMessageDAO | Outbound message access | - |
| localEmailMessageReceivedDAO | Inbound message storage | emailMessagesReceived |
| emailMessageReceivedDAO | Inbound message access | - |
| localEmailMessageProcessedDAO | Processed inbound storage | emailMessagesProcessed |
| emailMessageProcessedDAO | Processed inbound access | - |
| emailConfigDAO | Per-SPID config | emailConfig |
| emailServiceConfigDAO | Connection config | emailServiceConfig |

### Complete Data Flow

```
OUTBOUND EMAIL FLOW:
+-------------------+     +-------------------+     +-------------------+
| Application Code  |     | localEmailMessage |     | Rule Engine       |
| creates           |---->| DAO               |---->| processes         |
| EmailMessage      |     | (status: DRAFT)   |     | (status: UNSENT)  |
| (status: DRAFT)   |     |                   |     |                   |
+-------------------+     +-------------------+     +--------+----------+
                                                             |
                          +-------------------+              |
                          | SMTPAgent or      |<-------------+
                          | MSGraphAgent      |
                          | polls & sends     |
                          | (status: SENT/    |
                          |  FAILED)          |
                          +-------------------+

INBOUND EMAIL FLOW:
+-------------------+     +-------------------+     +-------------------+
| EmailFolderAgent  |     | emailMessage-     |     | Application       |
| polls IMAP        |---->| ReceivedDAO       |---->| processes         |
| folder            |     | (status: RECEIVED)|     | (status: PROCESSED|
+-------------------+     +-------------------+     +--------+----------+
                                                             |
                          +-------------------+              |
                          | emailMessage-     |<-------------+
                          | ProcessedDAO      |
                          | (archival)        |
                          +-------------------+
```

---

## Microsoft Graph Integration

### Configuration Requirements

To use Microsoft Graph for sending emails:

1. **Azure AD Application Setup:**
   - Register an application in Azure AD
   - Grant `Mail.Send` permission (application permission)
   - Create a client secret
   - Note the client ID and tenant ID

2. **EmailServiceConfig Setup:**
   - Create entry with `class: foam.core.notification.email.ms.EmailServiceConfig`
   - **CRITICAL:** Use `id: 'msGraph'` (not 'msGraphConfig' or other names)
   - Set `clientId`, `tenantId`, `password` (client secret), `username` (sending address)

3. **Agent Configuration:**
   - The `microsoftGraphEmailAgent` service references config with `id: 'msGraph'`
   - Set `enabled: true` in services.jrl to activate

### ID Matching Requirement

```
+----------------------------------+     +----------------------------------+
| MicrosoftGraphEmailAgent         |     | ms.EmailServiceConfig            |
|                                  |     |                                  |
| properties:                      |     | Journal Entry:                   |
|   id: {                          |     |   id: 'msGraph'  <-- MUST MATCH  |
|     class: 'Reference',          |---->|   clientId: '...'                |
|     value: 'msGraph'  <--        |     |   tenantId: '...'                |
|   }                              |     |   password: '...'                |
+----------------------------------+     +----------------------------------+
```

---

## Gotchas

### 1. EmailServiceConfig ID Mismatch

**Issue:** Microsoft Graph emails not sending; agent can't find config.

**Solution:** The `MicrosoftGraphEmailAgent` looks for config with `id: 'msGraph'` (not 'msGraphConfig'). Ensure your config entry uses `id: 'msGraph'` exactly.

### 2. Template Not Found

**Issue:** Email body is empty or uses wrong template.

**Solution:** Check template lookup order:
- Template must have matching `name` or `id`
- Group must match user's group or be `*`
- Locale must match or fall back to `en`
- SPID must match or be empty

### 3. Rule Not Triggering

**Issue:** Email stuck in DRAFT status.

**Solution:** Ensure the email rules are enabled in `rules.jrl`. The rules trigger on PUT to `localEmailMessageDAO` when `status=DRAFT`.

### 4. Agent Not Starting

**Issue:** Emails stuck in UNSENT status.

**Solution:**
- Check `EmailServiceConfig.enabled` is `true`
- Agent services have `lazy: false` - they start at boot
- Check EventRecord DAO for startup/error events

### 5. Template Variables Not Replaced

**Issue:** Email shows `{{ variableName }}` instead of value.

**Solution:**
- Ensure variable is in `templateArguments` map
- Check for typos in variable names
- Variable names support alphanumeric, dash, caret, underscore only
- For object properties, use `{{ object.property }}` syntax

### 6. Attachments Not Working

**Issue:** Attachments missing from sent email.

**Solution:**
- Attachments are file IDs (strings), not file objects
- Files must exist in `fileDAO`
- Both `IdentifiedBlob` and `InputStreamBlob` are supported

### 7. Rate Limiting

**Issue:** Emails failing with "Too many login attempts" or similar.

**Solution:**
- SMTP default throttle: 14 TPS (smtpAgentThrottle)
- MS Graph default throttle: 4 TPS (microsoftGraphEmailAgentThrottle)
- Adjust `foam.core.pool.Throttle.rate` if needed

### 8. SVG Images in Emails

**Issue:** SVG images not displaying in email clients.

**Solution:** The `EmailMessagePropertyServiceRuleAction` automatically replaces `.svg` extensions with `.png` in the body. Ensure PNG versions exist at same paths.

### 9. IMAP Delete vs Mark as Read

**Issue:** Emails reprocessed after restart.

**Solution:** Set `EmailServiceConfig.delete: true` to delete after processing. Default (`false`) only marks as SEEN, which may not persist across restarts with some providers.

---

## Related Documentation

- `foam3/doc/guides/email-setup.md` - Step-by-step setup guide
- `foam3/src/foam/core/notification/` - Notification system (often triggers emails)
- `foam3/src/foam/core/theme/` - Theme system (provides email styling context)

name: Enum
description: Covers FOAM Enums: declaring with foam.ENUM, ordinal/label/properties/methods, usage analogous to Java enums.

value.markdown:
<flow name="Enum" category="DOC/GUIDE" spid="foam" description="Covers FOAM Enums: declaring with foam.ENUM, ordinal/label/properties/methods, usage analogous to Java enums." keywords="enum,ordinal,label,values,knowledge"/>

# Enums

For those familiar with Java, FOAM Enums are very similar to Java enums in
design.

An Enum is essentially a class with a fixed number of named instances.
The instances are frequently referred to as Enum Values, or the 'values'
of an Enum.

Enums have most of the features available to FOAM classes, including
properties, methods, constants, templates, and listeners.

Enums extend from FObject, so they inherit FObject features such as
pub/sub events, diffing, hashCode, etc.

Enums also have a few built-in properties by default. Every Enum has an
'ordinal' property, which is a integer unique to all the Enum Values of a
particular Enum. Each enum also has a 'name' property, which is the name
given to each Enum Value.


## Example Usage:
To define an enum we use the `foam.ENUM()` function.
```js
foam.ENUM({
  name: 'IssueStatus',
  // Enums share many features with regular classes, the properties
  // and methods we want our enums to have are defined as follows.
  properties: [
    {
      class: 'Boolean',
      name: 'consideredOpen',
      value: true
    }
  ],
  methods: [
    function foo() {
      return this.label + ( this.consideredOpen ? ' is' : ' is not' ) +
          ' considered open.';
    }
  ],
  // Use the values: key to define the actual Enum Values that we
  // want to exist.
  values: [
    {
      name: 'OPEN'
    },
    {
      // The ordinal can be specified explicitly.
      name: 'CLOSED',
      ordinal: 100
    },
    {
      // If the ordinal isn't given explicitly it is auto assigned as
      // the previous ordinal + 1
      name: 'ASSIGNED'
    },
    {
      // You can specify the label, which will be used when rendering in a
      // combo box or similar
      name: 'UNVERIFIED',
      label: 'Unverified'
    },
    {
      // Values for additional properties to your enum are also defined
      // inline.
      name: 'FIXED',
      label: 'Fixed',
      consideredOpen: false
    }
  ]
});
```

```js
console.log(IssueStatus.OPEN.name); // outputs "OPEN"
console.log(IssueStatus.ASSIGNED.consideredOpen); // outputs "true"
```

Enum value ordinals can be specified.
```js
console.log(IssueStatus.CLOSED.ordinal); // outputs 100
// values without specified ordinals get auto assigned.
console.log(IssueStatus.ASSIGNED.ordinal); // outputs 101
```

Methods can be called on the enum values.
```js
// outputs "Fixed is not considered open."
console.log(IssueStatus.FIXED.foo());
```

To store enums on a class, it is recommended to use the Enum property type.
```js
foam.CLASS({
  name: 'Issue',
  properties: [
    {
      class: 'Enum',
      of: 'IssueStatus',
      name: 'status'
    }
  ]
});

var issue = Issue.create({ status: IssueStatus.UNVERIFIED });
console.log(issue.status.label); // outputs "Unverified"
```

Enum properties give you some convenient adapting. You can set the property to the ordinal or the name of an enum, and it will set the property to the correct Enum value.
```js
issue.status = 100;
issue.status === IssueStatus.CLOSED; // is true
```

Enum properties also allow you to assign them via the name of the enum.
```js
issue.status = "ASSIGNED"
issue.status === IssueStatus.ASSIGNED; // is true
```

The extent of all Enum values can be accessed from either the collection from any individual Enum value:
```js
console.log(IssueStatus.VALUES, IssueStatus.CLOSED.VALUES);
```

Values can be specified as just Strings if you don't want to explicitly the label or ordinal. 

```js
foam.ENUM({
 name: 'DaysOfWeek',
 values: [
   'SUNDAY',
   'MONDAY',
   'TUESDAY',
   'WEDNESDAY',
   'THURSDAY',
   'FRIDAY',
   'SATURDAY'
 ]
});
```

## Enums render as status badges

Every enum value already carries presentation properties: `label`, `color`, `background`, `borderColor`, `glyphFill`, `glyphBackground`, `icon`, `isBold`, `isItalic` and a `glyph` (`src/foam/lang/Enum.js:326-390`). An enum property's default view shows the read-only value through `foam.u2.view.ReadOnlyEnumView` (`src/foam/u2/view/EnumView.js:21-26`, `src/foam/u2/Element2.js:2273-2280`), which draws it as a coloured pill as soon as any value of that enum defines `color` or `background` (`ReadOnlyEnumView.js:94-99`).

So a status display needs no hand-made pill. Give the values colours, preferably `$` tokens (the view resolves them, `ReadOnlyEnumView.js:101-105`), and the pill appears wherever the property is shown read-only. `foam.core.app.HealthStatus` is a working example (`src/foam/core/app/HealthStatus.js:14-18`):

```js
foam.ENUM({
  package: 'demo',
  name: 'InvoiceStatus',
  values: [
    { name: 'OPEN',    label: 'Open',    color: '$statusSuccessText', background: '$statusSuccessBackground' },
    { name: 'OVERDUE', label: 'Overdue', color: '$statusDangerText',  background: '$statusDangerBackground' }
  ]
});
```

**`glyph` is taken.** Every enum gets a `glyph` property of class `GlyphProperty` (`Enum.js:375-377`). Declaring your own `glyph` property with another class replaces the built-in one, and a debug build warns `Change of Axiom ... type from GlyphProperty to String` (`src/foam/lang/debug.js:212-222`). Pick another name for your own field.

<flow name="EventRecord" category="DOC/DEV" spid="foam" label="Event Record" description="EventRecord (ER): logs a logical operation and can generate Alarms and Notifications based on severity and rules." keywords="eventrecord,alarm,notification,logging,knowledge"/>

# Event Record (ER)

# Overview

An EventRecord, as the name implies, notes a logical operation.  Generally a reoccuring operation such as a cronjob or EFT operation against a remote endpoint.

An EventRecord consolidates varius notifcations such as Logging, Alarms, Notifications, EmailMessages.

An EventRecord will always produce a Log Message, and depending upon Log Severity and Rule configuration, generate an Alarm and Notification.

The EventRecordDAO has Rule enabled, so any number of Rules can be crafted for many scenarios.  By default an EventRecord of severity WARN or ERROR will generate an Alarm and Notification.

# Intent

The EventRecordDAO is meant to be a single view for Operations to view the goings-on of an application.

# Use

As a minimum, an EventRecords requires an **event** string, and then optionally a **partner** and **code**.

## Example

### Error, Alarm event

```
DAO eventRecordDAO = (DAO) x.get("eventRecordDAO");
EventRecord er = new EventRecord(x, this, "event", "partner", "errorCode", "message", LogLevel.ERROR, new Exception("stacktrace"));
eventRecordDAO.put(er);
```

### General info event

```
DAO eventRecordDAO = (DAO) x.get("eventRecordDAO");
EventRecord er = new EventRecord(x, this, "event", "partner");
eventRecordDAO.put(er);
```

# Alarm Raise and Clear

Alarms are raised on WARN or ERROR level.  A raised Alarm will be cleared if an EventRecord of severity INFO is created with a matching **event**, **partner**, **code**.

# Event Record Response

An Event Record Response is a detailed description of an Event Record and what to do when one is encountered.

# Parsers 
FOAM includes parser libraries for both Java and Javascript.

They can be found in the foam.parse package.

The library provides a collection of what are called "parse combinators", which are simple
parsers which can be combined to form larger parsers. While this approach is unusual when
creating parsers, it is a proven technique in other domains, especially in GUI View libraries.
A large complex view like an email client or issue tracker is actually composed of simpler
views like buttons, text-fields, tab controls, etc. Parsers can be created by composing
simpler parsers, which are then themselves be composed into larger ones.

Parsers can be used anywhere a regular-expression could be, but are more powerful and can
be used in places where regular-expressions wouldn't be sufficient. Parsers are generally
not as compact as regular-expressions, but are easier to read.

Parsers can be used for many things, including:
1. extracting data from files
2. understanding network requests
3. validating and reformatting user input
4. creating languages, from small Domain-Specific-Languages (DSLs) to full-featured ones
5. source code linters, refactoring tools, or syntax highlighters

FOAM parsers accept input in the form of objects which implement the PStream interface.
PStream is short for "Parser Stream".


PStreams have the following interface:
    get int     pos   - The character position in the input stream.

    get Char    head  - The first character in the stream at the current position.

    get PStream tail  - A PStream for the next position in the input stream.

    get Object  value - 'Value' associated with this PStream.

    PStream setValue(Object value) - Creates a new PStream at the same position
        but with a new 'value'. The value is used to hold the result of a
        (sub-)parse.

PStreams are immutable, which greatly simplifies backtracking.

A Parser has the following interface:
    PStream parse(PStream stream);

It takes a PStream as input, and returns either a PStream
advanced to the point after all input is consumed by the parser,
or 'undefined' if the parse failed. The value generated by the parser
is stored in the .value property of the returned PStream.
## Simple Parsers First we'll start off by explaining the "simple" parsers. Simple parsers do not combine any other parsers, they do all of their parsing on their own. ## foam.parse.Parsers We use the foam.parse.Parsers Singleton class which provides convenience constructors for the various parser types. ## Literal Parser The simplest parser is a literal parser, which only parses the supplied string. // Create a Singleton for accessing the built-in Parser library var P = foam.parse.Parsers.create(); // Create an input PStream to parse our String var ps = foam.parse.StringPStream.create({str: 'abcdef'}); // Let's look at our PStream log(ps.toString()); // Now create a Literal Parser using the Singleton instance 'P' created above. // This parser will only parse the literal 'abc'. var lp = P.literal('abc'); // Now let's parse the PStream with the Parser ps = lp.parse(ps); // Now let's look at the results of our parsing log(ps.toString()); // If we try to parse 'abc' again notice that it will fail because the stream is now // at 'def', since 'abc' was consumed. var np = lp.parse(ps); log(!np?'undefined':np.toString()); // Here we'll create an in-lined literal 'def' parser and then call in directly. log(P.literal('def').parse(ps).toString()); ## Parser Tester Before continuing, let's write a helper function testP() to make demonstrating parser examples easier. The testP() function uses the U2 GUI library to create a table of input output pairs. For more information on the U2 library, please view the U2 examples. For our purpose though, you can treat this function as a blackbox that takes a parser and an array of strings to parse as input and displays the results in a table // Create a Singleton for accessing the built-in Parser library const P = foam.parse.Parsers.create(); // Function that invokes the parser for the given array of strs function testP(parser, strs) { globalThis.scope.br().start('table'). style({'min-width': '90%'}). attrs({border: 1, cellpadding: 6, cellspacing: 0}). start('tr').start('th'). style({background: '#eee'}). attrs({colspan:3}).add(`Parser: ${parser}`) .end(). end(). start('tr'). start('th'). add('Input'). end(). start('th'). add('Parsed'). end(). start('th'). add('Result'). end(). end(). forEach(strs, function(str) { // create a mutable slot for the input, this way we can change our examples on the fly var inputSlot = foam.lang.SimpleSlot.create({value: str}); // create another mutable slot to hold the parser output var outputSlot = inputSlot.map(input => parser.parse(P.stringPStream(input))); this.start('tr'). start('td'). style({width:'25%'}). tag({class: 'foam.u2.TextField', size: 10, onKey: true, data$: inputSlot}). end(). start('td').start('pre'). add(outputSlot.map(output => output ? str.substring(0, output.pos) : '')). end().end(). start('td').start('pre'). style({color: outputSlot.map(output => output ? 'green' : 'red')}). add(outputSlot.map(output => output ? JSON.stringify(output.value) : 'undefined')). end().end(). end(); }); } // Demonstrate the testP() function testP(P.literal('abc'), [ 'abc', 'abcdef', 'Abc', 'ABC', 'xyz' ]); // Store the test function and the singleton for the rest of the examples globalThis.P = P; globalThis.testP = testP; ## StringPStreams There's also a convenience method for creating StringPStreams in foam.parse.Parsers. Notice that the two StringPStreams appear identical, even though they are created in different ways. var ps = foam.parse.StringPStream.create({str: 'abc'}); log(ps.toString()); // Using the 'P' Singleton we created above. log(P.stringPStream('abc').toString()); ## Literal Ignore Case The literalIC() parser is like literal(), that we saw earlier, but it performs a case-insensitive match. Notice that it also parses 'Abc' and 'ABC', whereas the literal() didn't. testP(P.literalIC('abc'), [ 'abc', 'abcdef', 'Abc', 'ABC', 'xyz' ]); ## Any Char The anyChar() parser is the most indiscriminating parser. It will parse any one character. Notice that the only case where it fails to parse is when given an empty input. testP(P.anyChar(), [ 'abc', 'ABC', '!@#$%', '' ]); ## EOF EOF is a standard acronym for End Of File, but more generally it means the end of any input source. It is, in a way, the oppose of the anyChar() parser, since it won't parse any character except the EOF. testP(P.eof(), [ 'abc', 'ABC', '!@#$%', '' ]); ## Chars Parser The chars() parser will parse any single character which is included as part of the supplied string. testP(P.chars('abc'), [ 'ax', 'bx', 'cx', 'xb', '' ]); ## Not Chars Parser The notChars() parser will parse any single character which is NOT included as part of the supplied string. However, it will not parse EOF. testP(P.notChars('abc'), [ 'ax', 'bx', 'cx', 'xb', '' ]); ## Range Parser The range() parser is similar to chars(), except that it lets you more easily specify a range of characters. testP(P.range('0', '9'), [ 'a', '1', '2', '3', '9', 'z' ]); // Is short form for: testP(P.chars('0123456789'), [ 'a', '1', '2', '3', '9', 'z' ]); // It is often used to detect numbers (like above) or letters, like: testP(P.range('a', 'z'), [ 'a', '1', '2', '3', '9', 'z' ]); // Notice that it still only matches a single character testP(P.range('a', 'z'), [ 'abc', '123' ]); ## Combinators The above parsers are all simple parsers. They all parse a single character or a literal string. Now we'll look at combining the above simple parsers with parse combinators to create more complex parsers. ## Sequence Parser The most common parse combinator is the sequence parser, which combines multiple parsers into a single parser which only parses if each of the composed parsers successfully parses in sequence. Each parser picks up where the previous parser left off in the input stream. The sequence parser will fail if any of the composed parsers fails to parse. On a successful parse, the returned value is an array of the parsed values of each composed parser. // The first parser accepts a letter and the second parser accepts a number. var p = P.seq(P.range('a','z'), P.range('0','9')); testP(p, [ 'r2', 'd2', '3p', 'xy' ]); ## Literal Parser Shortcut In the example below, notice that we have three calls to P.literal(). Since P.literal() is so commonly used when creating parsers, we make it the default when you just pass a String to another parse combinator, like seq(). const TESTS = [ 'axxx', 'abxxx', 'abcxxx' ]; // The longer explicit method: testP(P.seq(P.literal('a'), P.literal('b'), P.literal('c')), TESTS); // A shorter more readable method: testP(P.seq('a', 'b', 'c'), TESTS); ## String Parser In one of the previous examples, when we demonstrated the sequence parser seq(), parsing 'r2' resulted in the parsed value of `[ 'r', '2' ]`, an array. However, we often want the result of our parsers to be string values, not the arrays of characters or substrings that were parsed by the individual parsers that comprised the sequence parser. To facilitate this, we use a very simple combinator parser called str() that decorates a single parser. Instead of changing that delegate parser's behaviour, it just changes its resulting value so that if it returns an array, it converts it into a single string value with the array values concatenated. // Notice unlike above, our results are strings, not arrays var p = P.seq(P.range('a','z'), P.range('0','9')); testP(P.str(p), [ 'r2', 'd2', '3p', 'xy' ]); ## Substring Parser 
The String parser shown above takes an array of parsed string values an concatenates them
into a single string return value. However, it is often the case that this isn't actually
what you want. Consider two cases where using str() is undesirable:
1. Sometimes you have multiple levels of string arrays and you would need to insert a str()
at each level.
2. You want to preserve input that has been lost, like the delimiters in a repeat().

Consider the following example which parses a sentence, which is a list of words separated
by whitespace. If you wanted to return the parsed string you would need to add a str()
around the 'word' parser so that you get strings instead of arrays of characters and then
you would need to add another str() around the repeat() in 'sentence'. But even this wouldn't
work because repeat() would have removed the whitespaces.

To solve this problem there is the substring() parse combinator which just returns the input
string that was parsed, as is, ignoring the return value of the composed parser.

???: perhaps input() would be a better name than substring()
var word = P.str(P.plus(P.range('a','z'))); const whitespace = P.plus(' '); const sentence = P.repeat(word, whitespace); const input = [ 'abc', 'abc def', 'abc def xyz' ]; // returns an array of words testP(sentence, input); // returns a single string of the words concatenated, without spaces testP(P.str(sentence), input); // preserves the original input testP(P.substring(sentence), input); // Notice that the str() on 'word' isn't needed when using substring(). var word = P.plus(P.range('a','z')); testP(P.substring(sentence), input); ## Alternate Parser The next most common parse combinator after the sequence parser, is the alt() parser. It's job is to take multiple delgate parsers, just like seq(), but to succeed if any of them succeed. It tries parsing with each composed parser in turn, and returns the result of the first one that succeeds. testP(P.alt(P.literal('A'), P.literal('B')), [ 'A', 'B', 'C' ]); // Or just: testP(P.alt('A', 'B'), [ 'A', 'B', 'C' ]); ## Repeat The repeat() parser takes a single delegate parser and repeatedly uses it to parse the input stream until it fails. The result of all delegate parses are combined in an array. testP(P.repeat(P.range('0','9')), [ '1', '1x', '123xyz', 'abc' ]); // Same example with the values converted into strings testP(P.str(P.repeat(P.range('0','9'))), [ '1', '1x', '123xyz', 'abc' ]); ## Plus You might have noticed that in the above example, repeat(0-9) succeeded in parsing the string 'abc' and provided an empty string result "" since there was no match. This is because repeat() parses zero or more occurrences of the delegate parser, so failure is a valid option. However, it's often the case that you want to consider a repeated parser to have succeeded when it parses one or more times. For this, there's the plus() parser, which behaves just like repeat(), but fails in the case where the delegate parses 0 times. testP(P.str(P.plus(P.range('0','9'))), [ '1', '1x', '123xyz', 'abc' ]); ## Delimited Repeat It's common to want to use repeat() to parse some pattern where each entry is separated by some other pattern. Examples include a comma separated list or semi-colon separated program statements. While you could do this by including the delimiter with seq() in the delegate parser, this is so common an operation that repeat supports it directly. // First lets' look how we would parse a comma delimited list of letters without using this feature: testP( P.str(P.repeat(P.str(P.seq(P.range('a','z'), P.literal(','))))), [ 'a', 'a,b', 'a,b,c', 'a,b,c,' ]); // Notice that the above never parsed the last letter, except for the last case: 'a,b,c,' // because there's a bug in our parser. We only want the comma between letters, not after, // which prevents the last 'c' from being parsed. // To fix this, we need to make our parser more complicated: testP( P.str(P.seq(P.str(P.repeat(P.str(P.seq(P.range('a','z'), P.literal(','))))), P.range('a', 'z'))), [ 'a', 'a,b', 'a,b,c', 'a,b,c,' ]); // This fixes that problem, but our parser is getting more complicated. Also, // notice that it is including the commas in the parsed output, but we probably // just want the letters. // The solution is to specify the delimiter to repeat(): testP( P.str(P.repeat(P.range('a','z'), ',')), [ '', 'a', 'a,b', 'a,b,c', 'a,b,c,' ]); // By supplying the delimiter parser as the second argument to repeat(), it knows that we // only want to skip delimiters between values and it excludes them from the output. // It is also shorter and easier to understand than our first attempt. // You can also specify a delimiter parser with plus(), in cases where you only want // the parse to succeed when you have one or more parses. testP( P.str(P.plus(P.range('a','z'), ',')), [ '', 'a', 'a,b', 'a,b,c', 'a,b,c,' ]); ## Repeat with a Number of Repetitions The repeat() parses zero or more times and plus() repeats one or more times, but sometimes you want to parse with some minimum number of repeats other than zero or one. The third optional argument of repeat() let's you specify just that. Since the second argument is the delimiter parser, if you don't want to have a delimiter, pass 'undefined' as its value. The below example checks passwords to ensure that they're at least five characters long. Notice that the repeat() parser still continues until it fails, hence for the last sample it repeated six times, meaning that the specified repeat parameter is the miniumum number of repetitions not the absolute limit. testP( P.str(P.repeat(P.alt(P.range('a','z'), P.range('A', 'Z'), P.range('0', '9'), P.anyChar('!@#$%^&*')), undefined, 5, 7)), [ 's', 's@', 's@c', 's@C&', 's@C&t', 's@C&t1', 's@C&t123456' ] ); ## Not Parser The Not parser is unusual in that it suceeds only if it's delegate parser fails. var quote = P.literal('"'); var stringBody = P.str(P.repeat(P.not(quote, P.anyChar()))); var stringParser = P.seq(quote, stringBody, quote); testP(P.str(stringParser), [ '""', '"a"', '"abc13234$@#$"', '"abc"asfasdf"' ]); ## Seq1 Parser Notice that in the previous string parser example, our result value was an array where the first and last elements were the quote '"' characters, and the second element was the actual string value we wanted. We would like the output value to ignore the surrounding syntax and just return us the one inner value that we're interested in. This is common enough to warrant it's own parse combinator. Seq1 behaves just like the regular seq() parser except instead of returning an array of values parsed by the delegates, it only returns the return value of one parser, the index of which you specify as the first argument. By using seq1(1, ...) instead of seq(...) we tell the parser to ignore the quote parsers and just give us the result of the stringBody parser, which is at location 1 (starting at zero). var quote = P.literal('"'); var stringBody = P.str(P.repeat(P.not(quote, P.anyChar()))); var stringParser = P.seq1(1, quote, stringBody, quote); testP(stringParser, [ '""', '"a"', '"abc13234$@#$"', '"abc"asfasdf"' ]); ## Until Parser The string pattern in the above example combined repeat(), not(), and anyChar() in order to extract the string. This pattern is common enough that we have a special parser for that called until(). It parses input until the delegated parser matches. We can use it to simplify the above stringParser. var quote = P.literal('"'); var stringParser = P.str(P.seq1(1, quote, P.until(quote))); testP(stringParser, [ '""', '"a"', '"abc13234$@#$"', '"abc"asfasdf"' ]); ## Optional Parser The optional() parser composes a single delegate parser and if that parser parses, then it returns its result, otherwise it returns the PStream as is, without failing. This lets parsing continue from the same point. testP(P.seq(P.optional('header'), 'body'), [ 'headerbody', 'body', 'header' ] ); ## Example The following example uses optional() several times to create a phone number parser where the long distance '1', the area code, and some punctuation are all optional. Notice that the parser also uses the str() combinator in several spots to ensure the final output is a string rather than an array. Notice this line: P.optional(P.literal('-'), '-'), We can specify a second parameter to optional() that returns the value to be used if the parser doesn't parse. In this case, we just want the add '-' if it wasn't present, to standardize the output format of the parser. var digit = P.range('0', '9'); var areaCode = P.str(P.seq('(', digit, digit, digit, ')')); var phoneNumber = P.str(P.seq( P.optional('1'), P.optional(' '), P.optional(areaCode), P.optional(' ', ' '), P.str(P.seq(digit, digit, digit)), P.optional('-', '-'), P.str(P.seq(digit, digit, digit, digit)) )); testP(phoneNumber, [ '1 (555) 555-1234', '1(555) 555-1234', '(555) 555-1234', '(555)555-1234', '555-1234', '5551234' ]); ## Optimizations ## Repeat0 
Some parsers end with the suffix '0'. This means they are specialized to not return any
value. This may seem unnecessary, and from a strict feature point of view, it is, but
the advantage of this type of parser is that it is more efficient because it performs
less work and generates less garbage. Parser performance can be very important because
it is often the most expensive operation performed by many applications.

In this example we use the repeat0() parser to parse whitespace. We don't care about
the whitespace, so we don't really care about the size or formation of the whitespace
and just want to skip over it efficiently. This is common for programming languages
where a significant portion of the input may be whitespace, and yet we don't need to extract
any values from the whitespace. We just want to skip over it as quickly and efficiently
as possible.
const whitespace = P.repeat0(P.chars(' \t\n'), null, 1); const word = P.str(P.plus(P.range('a', 'z'))); const words = P.repeat(word, whitespace); testP(words, [ 'abc', 'word word abc xyz', `word word on another line and more ` ]); ## Seq0 and Until0 Just as repeat0() is the no-value version of repeat(), seq0() is the no-value version of seq() and until0() is the no-value version of until(). We use both seq0() and until0() in this example to parse C-style `/* comments */`. For a language compiler we might throw away the contents of comments, so this type of parser might make sense. var comment = P.seq0('/*', P.until0('*/')); testP(comment, [ '/* This is a comment. Ignore the results. */' ]); // If you wanted the comment contents, then you would do: var comment = P.seq1(1, '/*', P.str(P.until('*/'))); testP(comment, [ "/* This is a comment. Don't ignore the results. */" ]); ## Example: Boolean Consider the following simple parser which is meant to parse boolean true or false values: var booleanParser1 = P.alt('true', 'false'); testP(booleanParser1, [ 'true', 'false' ]); // The above booleanParser1 works, but isn't ideal because the values it returns are // the string values "true" and "false", but since we are parsing booleans, we would // probably prefer getting back the actual boolean true and false values (ie. actual booleans // not strings). // This second version is almost the same but it specifies a second optional argument // to literal() which substitutes the value to be returned instead of the specified // string literal, in the event that the parse succeeds. var booleanParser2 = P.alt(P.literal('true', true), P.literal('false', false)); testP(booleanParser2, [ 'true', 'false' ]); // Now we get actual true and false values rather than "true" and "false". ## Grammars: Parenthesis Matching 
All of the above examples could have also been done with regular-expressions, but this
is the first example of something which can be parsed by a general-purpose parser but
could not be parsed with a regular-expression.

In this example we detect if a group of parenthesis is matched. To do so, the definition
needs to be recursive, which cannot be done with regular expressions. Notice that the
definition of 'parens' makes reference to itself with the sym('parens') parser.

When making recursive or more complex parsers, it is common to combine the individual
parsers into what is called a 'Grammar'. A grammar is a collection of mutually recursive
named parsers which together form a higher-level parser. A grammar is similar to how
many methods are combined in a single class in OO programming. Because grammars and OO
classes are so similar, FOAM uses classes to represent grammars.

To create a Grammar, you create a foam.CLASS which extends 'foam.parse.Grammar' and then
create a 'grammar' method which returns the grammar as JS map. The name you give each
parser in the map you return is called its symbol name. In the example below these are 'START' and 'parens'.
You reference a named parser using the sym() parser, like sym('parens'), in the example.
In that case, it is referencing itself. The symbol named 'START' is special because it
represents the default top-level parser for your grammar. When we use the MatchedParensParser,
it is the START parser which is used.

Notice that any of the parsers described previously are made available to the grammar
method as parameters. This is done to minimize syntax and make the resulting grammar easier
to read.

Parser grammars are normally defined in Extended Backus–Naur form (EBNF), which is similar
enough to FOAM Grammars to make conversion easy.
foam.CLASS({ name: 'MatchedParensParser', extends: 'foam.parse.Grammar', methods: [ function grammar(str, sym, eof, repeat, seq, seq1) { return { START: seq1(0, sym('parens'), eof()), // The 'repeat' allows for ()'s to be side-by-side, like ()() or (()()) parens: str(repeat( str(seq('(', sym('parens'), ')')), )) }; } ] }); var p = MatchedParensParser.create(); testP(p, [ // Matched '', '()', '(())', '()()', '((())()(()))', // Unmatched ')(', '(()', '())' ]); ## Grammars: Phone Number Parser While the above Grammar had only a single rule 'parens', it is more common for a grammar to have multiple rules, as in this example which implements a telephone number parser. foam.CLASS({ name: 'PhoneNumberParser', extends: 'foam.parse.Grammar', methods: [ function grammar(alt, sym, seq1, seq, str, literal, optional, plus, range) { return { START: str(seq( optional(sym('countryCode')), alt( str(seq(sym('areaCode'), optional(' ', ' '), sym('simple'))), sym('simple')) )), simple: str(seq(sym('prefix'), optional(sym('separator'), '-'), sym('line'))), digit: range('0', '9'), countryCode: seq1(1, optional('+'), literal('1', '1 '), optional(' ')), areaCode: str(seq( optional('(', '('), sym('digit'), sym('digit'), sym('digit'), optional(')', ')'))), prefix: str(seq( sym('digit'), sym('digit'), sym('digit') )), separator: alt('-', ' '), line: str(seq( sym('digit'), sym('digit'), sym('digit'), sym('digit') )) }; } ] }); var p = PhoneNumberParser.create(); // A good way to test/debug Grammars to to test each symbol individually: testP(p.getSymParser('countryCode'), [ '', '1', '+1', '+1 ' ]); testP(p.getSymParser('areaCode'), [ '', '555', '(555)', '55' ]); testP(p.getSymParser('prefix'), [ '', '12', '123', '1234' ]); testP(p.getSymParser('line'), [ '', '123', '1234', '12345' ]); testP(p, [ '+1 (555) 555-1234', '1 (555) 555-1234', '1(555) 555-1234', '(555) 555-1234', '555 555-1234', '15555551234', '5555551234', '(555)555-1234', '555-1234', '5551234' ]); ## Semantic Actions 
So far all of our parsers have mostly just returned the matched input but haven't actually
converted the input into anything else. While this is what is commonly done with
regular-expressions, parsers typically convert the input into something useful.
For an example a parser for the language 'C' might convert the source code input
into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) that is used by later stages of the compiler,
or a calculator expression parser might convert an arithmetic expression into
the result of that calculation.

This is done by what are called "Semantic Actions", which are just map functions which
are applied to the parser result to transform it into some other value.

Below is a very simple example which only adds one semantic action to our Grammar.
In this case it adds an action to the 'number' symbol so that numbers are converted
to actual JS numbers, rather than being left as Strings.

Semantic Actions are defined by creating a method named <SymbolName>Action. So in this
example, the 'numberAction' method is applied to results parsed by the 'number' parser.
foam.CLASS({ name: 'VersionParser', extends: 'foam.parse.Grammar', methods: [ function grammar(alt, not, sym, seq, str, optional, plus, repeat, range, anyChar) { return { START: repeat(sym('component'), optional(sym('separator'))), component: alt(sym('number'), sym('string')), digit: range('0', '9'), number: str(plus(sym('digit'))), string: str(plus(not(alt(sym('digit'), sym('separator')), anyChar()))), separator: alt('.', '-') }; }, function numberAction(v) { return parseInt(v); } ] }); var p = VersionParser.create(); testP(p, [ '1', '1.1', '1.1b', '3.14159-26b' ]); ## Email Address Parser The following parser uses two semantic actions to parse email addresses which can be either simple like "john@email.com" or labelled like "John Doe <john@email.com>". ## Match and MatchAll 
Usually parsers consume the entire input, but they can also be used like regexes to find
one or multiple instances in a larger input. Calling .match() on a Grammar will find the first
instance in the input text, whereas matchAll() will return an array of all matches.

The following example uses the previous PhoneNumberParser to extract one or more phone numbers
from an input text.
var p = PhoneNumberParser.create(); var input = 'blah blah blah (555) 123-4556, +1 (555) 123-1234 blah blah blah 555-1234 blah blah'; log('One:', p.match(input)); log('All:', p.matchAll(input).join(', ')); ## Grammar Reuse 
Typical parser generators like YACC (Yet Another Compiler Compiler) do not offer very good
mechanisms for reuse, but Object-Oriented (OO) programmers are used to having inheritance and composition
for this purpose. Inheritance allows a class to derive properties and behavior from a parent class,
enabling code reuse and specialization. Composition, on the other hand, involves building complex
functionality by combining simpler, independent components, promoting modularity and flexibility.

FOAM Grammars nicely bring the worlds of high-level parser specifications and OO together,
so that you can have the advantages of modern OO languages while writing your grammars.

This example demonstrates reuse through both composition and inheritance. The example is of a
simple expression parser and interpreter derived from the built-in base defined in:
scaleParser.js.

For composition, we create a NumberParser which is only able to parse negative or positive
integers. This class/grammar isn't very large, but by the time we add support for
decimal places, exponents, and maybe even numbers expressed in different bases, this class
could become fairly large. It makes the code more modular and reusable to keep isolated
features in their own classes. This way we could reuse the NumberParser in other classes,
or could have different versions (say a JS version or a Java version) and then
choose between implementations if we wanted to support JS or Java style
numbers.

To illustrate inheritance, we first create a generic ExpressionParser, and then we inherit from
it to create an ExpressionInterpreter. Grammars can be large and complex, and represent
a sizeable investment of effort, so you might want to use the same grammar for multiple
purposes. For example, our ExpressionParser might be used for an expression linter, pretty-printer,
interpreter (as we've done), JS compiler (compile to JS syntax), Java compiler, etc.

As an example, imagine you were writing a tool that linted both EcmaScript versions 14 and 15.
These too languages are mostly the same, but not identical. You could write two separate
parsers and linters, or you could use inheritance and composition to reuse most of the code,
keeping your codebase smaller and more maintainable. And then when the next version of
EcmaScript comes, your could quickly add support by reusing the code and parsers you already have.

This example is also interesting because it demonstrates a common use of parsers, which is
creating languages. Implementing a new language might seem like some kind of
deep magic, but as you can see in this example, the basic concept isn't difficult.
While we just create a simple expression interpreter, the same techniques
could be used to make a full fledged language interpreter.
const input = [ '123', // number '-123', // number '(123)', // group 'sqrt(9)', // fun 'log2(64)', // fun 'x', // variable 'y', // variable 'z', // variable '1+2', // expr '1+2+3', // expr '1*2', // expr1 '2^4', // expr2 '1*(x+y*sqrt(9))*-23/4', 'abc' // bad input ]; // A simple parser for negative or positive integers foam.CLASS({ name: 'NumberParser', extends: 'foam.parse.Grammar', methods: [ function grammar(plus, sym, alt, seq1, range, str) { return { START: alt(sym('positive'), sym('negative')), positive: str(plus(range('0', '9'))), negative: seq1(1, '-', sym('positive')) }; }, function positiveAction(s) { return parseInt(s); }, function negativeAction(n) { return -n; } ] }); // A generic Expression Parser. It will just tell you if the expression is valid, // but does not do anything to evaluate it. foam.CLASS({ name: 'ExpressionParser', extends: 'foam.parse.Grammar', requires: [ 'NumberParser' ], methods: [ function grammar(plus, sym, alt, opt, seq, seq1, lit, range, eof) { return { START: seq1(0, sym('expr'), eof()), expr: seq(sym('expr1'), opt(seq(alt('+', '-'), sym('expr')))), expr1: seq(sym('expr2'), opt(seq(alt('*', '/'), sym('expr1')))), expr2: seq(sym('expr3'), opt(seq1(1, '^', sym('expr2')))), expr3: alt( sym('fun'), sym('variable'), sym('number'), sym('group')), variable: alt('x', 'y', 'z'), fun: seq( alt('sqrt', 'log2'), '(', sym('expr'), ')' ), group: seq1(1, '(', sym('expr'), ')'), number: this.NumberParser.create() }; } ] }); const p = ExpressionParser.create(); testP(p, input); // An Expression interpreter. Extends the parser above to implement an interpreter/calculator // which evaluates the supplied expressions. foam.CLASS({ name: 'ExpressionInterpreter', extends: 'ExpressionParser', properties: [ 'x', 'y', 'z' ], methods: [ function exprAction(v) { if ( v[1] === null ) return v[0]; if ( v[1][0] == '+' ) return v[0] + v[1][1]; return v[0] - v[1][1]; }, function expr1Action(v) { if ( v[1] === null ) return v[0]; if ( v[1][0] == '*' ) return v[0] * v[1][1]; return v[0] / v[1][1]; }, function expr2Action(v) { if ( v[1] === null ) return v[0]; return Math.pow(v[0], v[1]); }, function funAction(v) { return v[0] == 'sqrt' ? Math.sqrt(v[2]) : Math.log2(v[2]) ; }, function variableAction(v) { return this[v]; } ] }); const interp = ExpressionInterpreter.create({x: 1, y: 10, z: 100}); testP(interp, input); // We could extend ExpressionParser again to implement a pretty-printer or a compiler ## Another Reuse Example Imagine we wanted to create a calculator for working with binary numbers. Rather than starting from scratch, we can reuse our existing ExpressionInterpreter and just swap out the default decimal NumberParser with a new BinaryNumberParser. const input = [ '1', // number '0', // number '-101', // number '(101)', // group '1+10', // addition '10*100', // addition '101+111+1' // addition ]; foam.CLASS({ name: 'BinaryNumberParser', extends: 'foam.parse.Grammar', methods: [ function grammar(plus, sym, alt, seq1, range, str) { return { START: alt(sym('positive'), sym('negative')), positive: str(plus(range('0', '1'))), negative: seq1(1, '-', sym('positive')) }; }, function positiveAction(s) { return parseInt(s, 2); }, function negativeAction(n) { return -n; } ] }); foam.CLASS({ name: 'BinaryInterpreter', extends: 'ExpressionInterpreter', requires: [ 'BinaryNumberParser as NumberParser' ] }); const interp = BinaryInterpreter.create({x: 1, y: 10, z: 100}); testP(interp, input); ## Error Reporting 
All of the examples until now have simply returned undefined if the input could not be
parsed, but it would be much better to be able to report an error message which
explained why the input could not be parsed. We do this with the ErrorReportingPStream.

Recall that PStream is an interface, but notice that the StringPStream is the
only implementation that we've seen so far. The ErrorReportingPStream is a PStream
decorator that wraps another PStream (probably a StringPStream in JS) and figures
out where a parse error occurred and provides an error message explaining where the
parse failed and what was expected.
// TODO: The JS ErrorReportingPStream isn't as useful as the Java version and should be improved // TODO: finish this example /* unfinished class, breaking the page, temporarily commenting out var p = ExpressionParser.create(); var sps = P.stringPStream('1+2*(1+2'); // Missing closing ')' log('StringPStream:', p.parse(sps)); var erps = foam.parse.ErrorReportingPStream.create({ delegate: P.stringPStream('1+2*(1+2') }); var res = p.parse(erps, p); log('ErrorReportingPStream:', res); log(erps); */

description: Step-by-step instructions for exporting a Reflow flow from the running app and replacing it in the .jrl source file.

value.markdown:
<flow name="ExportingFlows" category="DOC/GUIDE" spid="foam" description="Step-by-step instructions for exporting a Reflow flow from the running app and replacing it in the .jrl source file." keywords="reflow,export,flow,jrl,knowledge"/>

# Exporting ("Lifting") Flows

When you build or edit a Reflow flow in the running app, it lives in the `flowDAO` on the
server. To capture it — to check it into source control, move it between environments, or hand
it to someone else — you "lift" it out of the DAO as text. This guide covers the reliable way to
do that from the UI.

## Steps

1. **Open Reflow.** Navigate to the Reflow console (search the app menu for **Reflow** and open
   it).

2. **Open the Flow DAO.** In the console, type:

   ```
   dao flow
   ```

   This runs the `dao` command against `flowDAO` and renders a table of every saved flow.

3. **Find the flow with a `where` clause.** The flow list can be long, so filter it with an
   [AQL](./AutoQueryParser.md) query in the DAO browser's search bar instead of scrolling. Match
   on the flow's `name`:

   ```
   name="PropertyBorder"
   ```

   Other useful filters:

   ```
   name~"Demo"          // contains "Demo"
   category="demos"     // all flows in the demos category
   ```

   The table narrows to the matching flow(s).

4. **Open the export in a new tab.** Select the flow's row and choose **Download**. Two format
   options appear:

   - **JSON** — a plain JSON representation of the flow object. Good for inspection, diffing, or
     tooling that expects JSON.
   - **J (journal)** — the journal form, i.e. the `p({ ... })` entry you see in a `.jrl` file.
     This is what a `flows.jrl` stores, so it is the one to use when updating the checked-in
     flow.

   Rather than saving a file, **right-click the format you want (JSON or J) and choose "Open Link
   in New Tab."** The raw text renders directly in the browser.

5. **Select all and copy.** In that new tab, select the entire contents (**Cmd+A** on macOS /
   **Ctrl+A** on Windows/Linux) and copy it (**Cmd+C** / **Ctrl+C**). This is the full,
   authoritative text of the flow.

6. **Replace the flow in its source file.** Open the flow's source `.jrl` (e.g.
   `foam3/src/foam/demos/u2/working-with-u2/flows.jrl`), locate the entry for this flow — find
   its `"name":"..."` — and replace that flow's `p({ ... })` block with the text you just copied.
   Save. On the next build the updated flow replays into `flowDAO`.

## Notes

- **Lift the whole flow, not just a block.** Exporting through `flowDAO` captures the complete
  flow — metadata (`name`, `label`, `version`, `category`), access control, and the full
  serialized `script` of blocks. Copying an individual block's text out of the editor loses this
  wrapper.
- **Version bumps.** Each save increments the flow's `version`. If you re-lift after editing,
  expect the `version` (and block contents) to differ from the copy you exported earlier — this
  is how the app detects that a stored flow is newer than a checked-in one.
- **Round-trip.** A lifted **J** entry can be dropped straight into a `flows.jrl` under the
  appropriate directory; it will be replayed into `flowDAO` on the next build. See
  [Journals](./Journals.md) for how `.jrl` files load.

## Related

- [Reflow](./Reflow.md) — the console, flows, and block model.
- [AutoQueryParser](./AutoQueryParser.md) — the `where`-clause query syntax used in step 3.
- [Journals](./Journals.md) — how exported **J** entries are loaded back.
